talks.title: Attacking Classified Safes & Vaults from the Cold War to Now
talks.teaser: Traces safe and vault attacks from Cold War espionage teams to modern lock manipulation and drilling.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a safe technician and physical security specialist, frames the talk around how classified containers are defeated in practice. He explains that a safe's real purpose is to make an attacker's effort so costly that the payoff is not worth it. He then walks through common countermeasures, including glass relockers, chemical traps, and hardened plates, and describes how technicians drill, repair, and conceal entry points in a container.

The middle of the talk is a history of attacks that do not leave obvious damage. It covers manipulation of lock wheels, vibration attacks that accidentally opened naval safes at sea, and duress codes and time locks. It also covers manipulation-resistant designs and the electromechanical locks that followed. A large thread concerns Cold War radiographic attacks, including a Polish espionage unit that used radioactive isotopes and film to read the wheels inside locks. The talk also describes a government lock whose weakness was known for years while its manufacturer worked to suppress the research.

The closing argument is that protection should match what is being guarded, and that personal valuables are better served by distributing copies across trusted places than by concentrating them in one container. The speaker ends by pointing listeners to follow-up discussion in the lockpick village.

talks.title: Meshtastic Attacktastic
talks.teaser: Shows how an off-grid Meshtastic radio mesh can be abused, and which controls reduce the risk.
talks.summary:
Meshtastic is an open-source platform for off-grid, long-range mesh messaging over LoRa radio, controlled from a phone app. The speaker explains how nodes relay messages hop by hop, where people use it on backcountry trips and during emergencies, and why the low-power hardware is cheap to deploy. The talk then turns to weak spots: small devices that can be stolen or hard to reach, GPS beaconing that reveals where a node sits and traces a person's movements, a default channel with trivial encryption, and shared private keys that are never rotated.

The main demonstration shows a dongle-based rig planted near a target. It relays commands over the mesh to a nearby machine, which then gets driven like a keyboard once a malicious USB device is plugged in. The speaker built on work by a colleague, framed it as educational, and noted that two antivirus products had to be removed before it would run. The demo opened calculator and Notepad on a Windows machine from a phone.

The closing advice is practical. Lock down physical access and use tamper-evident hardware. Prefer stronger keys, and manage them through a rotated, centrally generated source rather than passing a static key around. Turn off GPS when it is not needed, watch for rogue access points with wireless intrusion detection, keep firmware patched, and block USB ports.

talks.title: Building and Hacking USB with FPGAs
talks.teaser: Walks through open-source FPGA tools for building USB devices, analyzing USB traffic, and emulating hardware.
talks.summary:
The talk revisits the USB hardware work of Great Scott Gadgets, tracing how the earlier Daisho project, a super speed USB board, led to the smaller Cynthion analyzer. The speaker explains that Cynthion pairs an FPGA with open-source gateware, and that the Luna library, written in Amaranth HDL, provides the USB logic. Python scripts drive the build flow, so a new bitstream can be generated and loaded onto the board in seconds.

A large part of the talk covers Packetry, a Rust-based USB analyzer. Using live demos, the speaker compares it with Wireshark while capturing from a HackRF. The comparison shows that Linux usbmon exposes host controller requests rather than the traffic on the wire, and that Wireshark slows badly once a capture reaches millions of packets. An upcoming interleaved hierarchical view is previewed as a way to keep both protocol hierarchy and chronological order.

The later sections cover Facedancer, which lets a host Python script act as a USB device for a target computer, so the target sees a real device. A live example reverse engineers the board ID and version requests of a HackRF using the suggest feature. The closing part lists ways to build USB devices in software, gateware, or added hardware, and points listeners to the open-source projects and documentation behind them.

talks.title: Rayhunter Recording PCAPs from Stingrays With a 20 Ho
talks.teaser: Presents Rayhunter, a low-cost device that flags possible cell site simulators by analyzing LTE radio traffic.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at cell site simulators, also called stingrays or IMSI catchers, and why they are hard to detect on modern networks. The speakers trace how their interest began with protesters in North Dakota in 2016, then explain that earlier detection tools either relied on limited Android APIs or only watched 2G, which newer networks no longer use. Their first prototype, built on software-defined radios, was costly and produced misleading alerts because it depended on incomplete tower databases.

The second part introduces Rayhunter, an open project that runs on an inexpensive mobile hotspot with a Qualcomm baseband. It reads the modem's diagnostic stream, saves raw captures, and converts the radio messages into pcap files that Wireshark can dissect. Heuristics then scan the RRC and NAS layers for signs of downgrade attacks, null ciphers, and an identity request that the phone answers before the tower drops it, which the team calls the wallet inspector attack. Field tests at the border and around the DNC mostly found nothing, but a reanalysis of DNC data showed one pattern matching that attack, which the team says is strong evidence rather than proof.

The takeaway for practitioners is that cellular protocol logs can reveal surveillance, but the heuristics remain immature, NAS parsing is still missing, and false positives and negatives persist. The team asks for help with testing, interface design, and new detection rules, with the aim of putting the tool in the hands of journalists and activists.

talks.title: Windows Projected File System The Reality Stone
talks.teaser: Shows how the built-in Windows Projected File System can fake files on a host to alert defenders when attackers open them.
talks.summary:
The speaker presents a token type built on the Windows Projected File System, a feature included in later versions of Windows, as part of the open-source Canary Tokens project. The aim is to place placeholder files and folders that look real to anyone enumerating a host or a network share. Because the feature ships with Windows, defenders don't need to install an agent or extra software to deploy it.

The middle of the talk covers the internals. A provider runs a user-mode process, registers callbacks, and exposes a virtualization root, while reparse points mark which directories are projected. When an attacker opens or copies a decoy file, a callback receives the requesting process ID and the resolved path. The token then sends that information back as a base32-encoded DNS lookup. Directory enumeration is deliberately not alerted on, so that the signal stays high. The speaker also shows how to spot the feature with fsutil, tasklist and fltmc, and notes that these indicators also appear on legitimate systems.

The closing section raises open questions. The speaker asks for feedback on false positives from antivirus products and from tools such as ShareFinder and Snaffler, and suggests that callbacks could return different data depending on the calling process. The practical takeaway is that built-in Windows features can provide low-noise tripwires, and that offensive researchers will likely look for the markers that reveal projected directories. Reference C and PowerShell code is published on the project's GitHub page.

talks.title: Software Screws Around, Reverse Engineering Finds Out
talks.teaser: Argues that independent reverse engineering drives software accountability, using FTC enforcement cases as evidence.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a basic problem: it is hard to know what software actually does. Cloud-hosted components, silent updates and opaque AI features hide behavior from users, researchers and regulators. Trade secret doctrine makes this worse, since it can block access through public records exemptions, criminal discovery and misappropriation claims. The speakers frame software security as a credence good, a product whose quality buyers cannot judge without expert analysis, which they say leads to chronic underinvestment.

To test how much accountability depends on outside researchers, the team built a dataset from 102 privacy and security cases the Federal Trade Commission brought from 2017 onward, then traced how the agency first learned of each problem. About a quarter of the individual counts (26.5%) began with independent research, and more than a third of cases had at least one count tied to it. The share climbed sharply in cases about deceptive disclosure of data practices, where roughly two-thirds relied on outside analysis. Journalists, academics, industry staff and unaffiliated researchers all contributed.

The speakers argue that reverse engineering should be treated as a public good, that contracts barring analysis of critical technology such as voting machines should be restricted, and that gag orders and some bug bounty terms discourage disclosure. Their advice to researchers is to think carefully before joining bounty programs that buy silence. They released the dataset publicly and asked for reports of missed cases and errors.

talks.title: Taking Over Millions of Accounts from Abandoned Startups
talks.teaser: Shows how re-registering lapsed startup domains lets attackers reach old Google sign-in accounts at other services.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a skit about a fictional startup that shuts down while its domain lapses. The speaker then explains how "Sign in with Google" works: the service asks Google who a user is, Google confirms the email address, and the service logs that person in. Most sites only check the account's domain and email, so whoever buys an expired domain can recreate the same addresses and get into old accounts.

Using a public startup dataset, the speaker counted about 116,000 failed companies whose domains were available to buy. Registering one of them and creating a Google Workspace on it gave access to former employee accounts at several SaaS providers. One HR system exposed sensitive payroll and banking data. Some providers also leaked old user lists, which made the problem worse. The speaker estimates roughly ten million accounts could be affected. The Google subject identifier would be a stronger check, but it changes for some real users, so providers could not rely on it. Google first closed the report as working as intended, then reopened it with a small bounty and no concrete fix, past the usual 90-day disclosure window.

The speaker separates this from password reset flows, which providers can harden by adding a second verification step. Social login has no easy provider-side fix, since adding friction to login is unlikely to be accepted. The practical takeaway is to check whether sign-in relies only on email and domain, and to treat expired domains as an account takeover risk.

talks.title: Modern day SOC Evolution from Open Source to Unlimited Budget
talks.teaser: Walks through building a SOC from open-source tools to vendor platforms, drawn from years of running a conference network.
talks.summary:
The speakers, who run the security operations for a large conference network, trace how their setup grew from a single router and a few off-the-shelf parts in the early days to a team of more than 60 people serving about 25,000 attendees. As the event grew, cheap open-source scripts and hardware stopped scaling, so they began borrowing enterprise equipment from vendors in exchange for exposure.

The core of the talk walks through the building blocks they consider essential for a modern SOC: endpoint detection, central log storage in a SIM or data lake, network detection, orchestration and automation, threat intelligence platforms, sandboxing, behavior analytics, and identity controls. For each, they name leading commercial and open-source picks, drawn from informal polls of experienced practitioners, and weigh buying a product against staffing a team to run open tools. Real cases illustrate the points, including rental laptops with a compromised golden image caught by endpoint detection, an unknown HVAC system found through network traffic, and sensitive financial documents sent without encryption.

They close by explaining that hostile-looking traffic at a conference is mostly expected, so they tune alerts around classroom context and automate closure of benign detections. Their takeaways are to keep logs long enough to uncover long-running intrusions, validate what the network actually shows, be careful when baselining behavior, and expect AI assistants and insurance requirements to shape future SOCs.

talks.title: Deception & Operations Planning Frameworks
talks.teaser: Shows how to plan a deception operation, using a rural trespasser case study to illustrate a practical framework.
talks.summary:
Russell Handorf opens by arguing that many organizations still lack the basic controls that make defense work, and that buying a tool will not close that gap. He separates deception operations from honeypots, describing them as deliberate strategies that need clear planning. His framework asks planners to define the problem, the adversary they want to mislead, the duration, the budget and the level of complexity. It also asks how the operation will be dismantled without tipping off the adversary.

The middle of the talk is a case study from his own rural property, which had been unposted for decades and drew trespassers who hunted, shot, dumped trash and camped there. After standard measures such as gates, cameras and patrols, he created a fictional company with a website and signs carrying QR codes. Visitors who scanned a code were led through a collection flow that logged connection details useful for later legal follow-up, and a disclosure notice was added after talking with an attorney. He also describes problems, including an angry reaction from a neighbor and a visitor who ignored the signs.

He closes by stressing that deception requires sustained commitment, healthy baseline controls and a clear exit plan, and that it cannot be bought as a product. Some trespassers turned back while others did not, which he presents as partial success. The main takeaway for practitioners is to scope objectives, legal limits and wind-down steps before launching any deception effort.

talks.title: Detecting BLE Trackers
talks.teaser: Shows how to build a low-cost ESP32 device that detects nearby Bluetooth Low Energy trackers such as AirTags.
talks.summary:
The speakers open with a scenario from a domestic violence consultation, where a person felt tracked even though no one was following her. That framing sets up the question of how hidden location tags can be found. They explain that Bluetooth Low Energy advertisements are broadcast continuously, unlike classic Bluetooth's hidden hopping pattern, so a listener can pick up tracker beacons and follow their channel hops. Manufacturer identifiers inside the advertisement data let a scanner tell Apple devices apart, including AirTags versus iBeacons and registered versus unregistered tags, and recognize other brands.

The main build is a cheap ESP32-based display board, costing roughly eleven dollars, programmed through the Arduino IDE. The code checks each advertisement payload for known manufacturer IDs and reports what it finds on the screen and over serial. Bluetooth SIG company identifiers can extend coverage to other trackers, and the same method could flag devices such as vehicles or medical wearables, which raises privacy concerns. The speakers note that recent Android releases added built-in AirTag detection, but argue that a dedicated device is simpler for many people to configure.

The talk closes candidly about the prototype's limits: the display shows only a handful of results, serial output does not always match the screen, and only a few tracker types are supported. The speakers invite contributions to the open project and mention alternative firmware such as Marauder and Bruce that run on the same hardware. The takeaway is that the parts are cheap and the tooling is approachable, so anyone can build a practical tracker detector.

talks.title: Sandboxing Agentic Workflows with WASM
talks.teaser: Shows how to run LLM-generated Python in a browser sandbox using WebAssembly and Pyodide instead of on the server.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with agentic AI workflows, where an application lets a language model write code, runs it, and returns only the result. The speaker argues that several popular libraries execute that generated code directly on the application server, and that regex filters and naive exec calls give weak protection. The central point is that model output should be treated as untrusted, especially when users can influence what gets generated.

The speaker compares isolation options. Hypervisor-based sandboxes such as Firecracker and serverless platforms built on it are presented as the strongest server-side choice, while containers are judged weaker because they share the host kernel. The talk then proposes moving execution into the browser. A demo uses Pyodide, a CPython build compiled to WebAssembly, to run a plotting example and render an SVG. Browser permissions, network allowlists, memory limits, timeouts and output validation are presented as the controls that make this workable.

The talk closes with trade-offs. Runtime initialization is slow and heavy dependencies make installs painful, GPU code such as CUDA is hard to run in WebAssembly, and data not present on the client has to be embedded in generated code. Headless browsers are offered for cases where results must return to the server. The takeaway is that sandboxing decisions balance speed, user experience and security, and that many of the defenses are conventional ones applied to a new setting.

talks.title: Keeping Our Home Addresses Offline
talks.teaser: Explains why people-search listings keep resurfacing despite opt-outs and which policy changes could curb them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with how easily the speaker's own home address and personal details surfaced online, even after years of manual opt-outs. A person she challenged located her address within minutes through a paid people-search record she had not known existed. The talk frames this as an endless cycle in which removed listings reappear, and even privacy-focused professionals struggle to stay hidden.

The middle section covers a study run with Consumer Reports that tested paid data-removal services against manual opt-outs across 13 people-search sites. Results were mixed: some services performed noticeably better, but none removed everything, and information often came back weeks or months later. The speaker also points to conflicts of interest, where some removal firms have partnerships with the very sites they clean up.

The closing section argues that individual effort cannot solve this. State privacy laws often exempt publicly available data, which leaves major gaps. Proposed ideas include adding friction to bulk access to public records, making opt-outs easier to file in one place, and a pending federal rule that would treat data brokers as consumer reporting agencies. The takeaway is to push for policy change and to be realistic about what personal removal can achieve.

talks.title: A Commencement into Real Kubernetes Security
talks.teaser: Walks through how a benchmark-compliant Kubernetes cluster with no flagged CVEs can still be taken over through overprivileged roles.
talks.summary:
The speakers argue that many Kubernetes teams spend their effort on the wrong risks. Container breakouts, custom seccomp profiles and runtime security tools get most of the attention, yet they are costly to run well and are rarely what attackers use. They show that a seccomp profile built from a simple application's system call trace grew from 17 calls to nearly 1,900 once the app was packaged into a container, and that the resulting profile quietly allowed risky calls such as clone and BPF. Their point is that custom sandboxing is hard to get right and is mainly worth the effort for services that run untrusted customer code.

The main part of the talk is a live penetration test against a cluster that was hardened to the CIS benchmark, with no failing checks and no CVE findings. Starting from a notebook pod, the speakers found a service account token in another container's working directory because the pods shared a process namespace. That account could patch pods, which let them swap in their own image. A helper binary run on a node then harvested tokens and certificates from the host, and one account could create mutating admission webhooks. That allowed a sidecar to be injected into every new pod. They note that real criminals in this position are more likely to deploy cryptomining than to steal data, and a graph-based attack path tool confirmed the full route.

The takeaway is to focus first on role-based access control, on who can create pods or read secrets, and on admission control that blocks privileged pods and host namespaces. Counting CVEs in images matters less when the vulnerable code is never reached, and benchmark scores can create false comfort because many checks are manual. Teams should know their own threats and make the case for the right priorities to management and compliance.

talks.title: C2 Operators Infecting Themselves
talks.teaser: Shows how infostealer logs exposed command-and-control operators whose own machines were infected, revealing a malware ecosystem.
talks.summary:
Flare's researchers started with a database of more than 4,000 infostealer logs, all from victims who had visited a cybercrime forum. They used the Verbback C2 tracker, which lists over 11,000 known command-and-control hostnames, and expanded that list by about 8,000 more through DOM content matching. Checking the logs against these hostnames narrowed the pool to five machines that had reached a known C2. The infected devices were spread across Ukraine, Iran, Italy, the Netherlands and Hong Kong, all running Windows 10 or 11 and infected between 2023 and 2024.

Four of the five logs held several hundred credentials for mostly everyday websites. The fifth held only about 30, all tied to malicious activity, and its owner was nicknamed the Maestro. Its browsing history included administrative pages for the Raccoon infostealer back end, and its stored logins covered many panels. Three of the suspicious URLs matched known families: Mystic, Private Loader and a Trojan. The researchers read this as one operator running a layered toolkit, with a loader delivering payloads, a multifunction tool, an infostealer and a Trojan for persistence.

The talk's main lessons are that stealer logs can expose an operator's backstage activity, and that tracing known C2 endpoints may reveal indicators nobody had catalogued yet. That second method was not yet tested at scale. Attempts to identify the operator through their email addresses went nowhere. The speaker suggested that weak operational security, or malware bundled into cracked tools, could explain how the operator was infected.

talks.title: Disrupting the Model
talks.teaser: Shows how stolen cloud tokens let attackers steal models from MLOps platforms, and how to detect that activity.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the case that organizations are adopting machine learning platforms quickly, while the environments that train, tune, deploy and maintain models get little offensive or defensive attention. The presenters, from IBM X-Force Red, argue that the wider MLOps ecosystem, including data stores, orchestration, APIs and connected identity systems, is a valuable target that red teams should model. They note that commercial platforms often ship with audit logging and detections turned off, which leaves responders unprepared.

The middle section introduces a toolkit released alongside a white paper, which simulates REST API abuse against three commercial platforms using stolen access tokens or API keys. Live demos cover reconnaissance and model theft on Azure ML after a device code phishing scenario, and on Google Vertex AI after lateral movement to an engineer's workstation. Big ML was discussed but not demonstrated, and its cloud offering offers no logging to examine.

The closing advice focuses on threat modeling ML infrastructure, enabling audit logs, enforcing MFA, rotating credentials and applying least privilege. Defenders should watch for command and control beaconing from training environments and unusual lateral movement between platforms. The speakers also flag supply chain risk from untrusted model downloads, and point to detection content in the white paper such as queries, YARA and Sentinel rules.

talks.title: Taiwan Digital Blockade
talks.teaser: Shows how a wargame on a Taiwan blackout scenario surfaced ideas for resilient communications, power and civilian preparation.
talks.summary:
The talk comes from two research professors at a US naval college who wanted to know whether the approach Ukraine used after Russia's invasion could carry over to Taiwan. Ukraine's government leaned on private firms, service providers and security researchers to keep communications running and to push its own story to the outside world. Taiwan's situation was described as a small, densely connected island reliant on undersea cables, with an aging power system fed by imported fuel and a grid prone to blackouts after storms.

To test the idea, the speakers ran a wargame twice, once at a hotel and once on the DEF CON floor in the IC Village. About fifteen players, acting as advisers to the Taiwanese government, worked through a 2030 scenario that moved from cyber attacks, electronic warfare and cable sabotage to conventional strikes on power infrastructure. Teams then proposed investments for today, and players voted on the best ideas without being able to vote for their own team. Expected recommendations included cheap, widely spread communications gear and stockpiled spare parts. The more surprising theme was how much time players spent on civilian preparation, such as public education and volunteer repair networks. Some also suggested concentrating critical infrastructure in places an adversary might be less likely to attack.

The main takeaway is that resilience planning for a digitally dependent society involves people and institutions as much as hardware. The speakers closed by asking for invitations to Taiwan and for contacts with trusted people on the island or nearby who could supply real-world data to refine the findings.

talks.title: Lighting Up
talks.teaser: Delivers a 22-minute ShmooCon 2025 session framed around lighting up the event.

talks.title: OpSec for Grandma
talks.teaser: Shows how to protect older relatives from scams using Macs, DNS filtering, paper password books, and simple family rules.
talks.summary:
Rich Mogull starts from the point that security professionals often become unpaid IT support for their parents, relatives and friends. He says older family members are frequent targets, with scams arriving through email phishing, pop-ups served by ad networks, and cold calls or texts posing as tech support.

The middle of the talk lays out a five-part routine he says has nearly eliminated incidents in his own family over the past year. It begins with favouring Macs for their stronger default protections, and with locking Windows machines to the app store. Passwords go into a paper notebook, one account per page, written in simple characters that are easy to read. The most important control is a paid DNS filtering service run as a device agent, so protection follows the device off the home network and blocks malicious domains even when a link arrives by email. He also recommends a paid search engine rather than ad-funded search, and a few household rules: legitimate companies won't ask for passwords or bank details by phone or email, nothing gets installed on request, and relatives should call him rather than attempt fixes themselves.

In the Q&A he compares DNS options, saying a self-hosted Pi-hole needs too much upkeep, and recommends iOS for phones while warning against installing configuration profiles. The takeaway is that one trusted person maintaining low-friction defaults protects relatives better than expecting them to spot scams on their own.

talks.title: SQLi is so Last
talks.teaser: Shows how Postgres roles, stored procedures and in-database JWT checks can limit what SQL injection is able to reach.
talks.summary:
The talk asks why SQL injection keeps appearing despite prepared statements and ORMs. The speaker argues that prepared statements do not help if an attacker steals database credentials or finds a bug elsewhere, and that some ORMs have had injection flaws too. A core problem is that applications often connect as a powerful database role that can run arbitrary SQL.

The proposed remedy treats the database as an API. The application role receives execute rights only on security-definer functions that perform fixed operations, with row-level limits where needed. A stateless JWT, validated inside Postgres by an extension, lets the database itself decide who is calling rather than trusting the application server. A profile-update example shows the pattern end to end.

The speaker is candid about limits. Exposing the database directly is possible but largely untested, and a stored procedure that uses dynamic execute can itself be injectable, so static analysis and restricted roles remain important. Greenfield projects suit this best, though existing systems can migrate gradually. The takeaway is to shrink what a compromised query can reach rather than rely on one control.

talks.title: The Tech That Fought Back
talks.teaser: Shows how exposed political party and campaign websites leak personal data, and how trusted partners can drive fixes.
talks.summary:
Andrew Schoka describes his effort to examine the websites of political parties and campaigns across the United States, a set that grew to tens of thousands of domains. He built a tool, released publicly, to crawl these sites and pull out private contact details exposed through embedded third-party widgets, leftover cloud file links and old hosting artifacts. Checking the results against breach collections, he found that many exposed accounts used weak or reused passwords, and that state Republican and Democratic sites looked remarkably alike in this respect. Smaller local campaigns showed much less technical maturity, and few had basic denial-of-service protection, which he framed as a systemic resourcing problem rather than a partisan one.

The second half focused on how to get campaigns to act. Security practitioners face a trust barrier, since a provider seen as aligned with one side will not be welcome with the other. He suggested working through people already trusted in the political space, and partnering with a nonprofit that could deliver guidance straight to campaigns, which worked far better than cold outreach. His lessons were to prioritise fixing problems over only reporting them, to avoid working alone, to find internal champions inside organisations, and to offer skills locally.

For practitioners, the takeaway is that exposed contact data and weak credentials on small public-facing sites are common, and that remediation depends on credible messengers as much as technical findings.

talks.title: 0wn the Con Growing Up
talks.teaser: Organizers and their children explain how a volunteer-run hacker conference is built, funded, and finally wound down.
talks.summary:
This closing session looks behind the scenes of a long-running East Coast hacker conference as its organizers prepare to end it. The organizers explain that the event is run by a for-profit company rather than a nonprofit, and they estimate that the work adds up to several person-years of staff and volunteer effort. They say they chose to stop around the twenty-year mark on their own schedule, and a pandemic delay gave them one extra year.

The middle of the talk covers how the program is assembled. The call for papers drew roughly 249 submissions, which were scored in a review platform and then refined by a small group that balances tracks and reviewer variance. The speakers stress following submission instructions, asking organizers questions before submitting, and citing earlier work on a topic. They also explain that ticketing was kept in-house to limit how much attendee data is shared, and that sponsorship is capped so sponsors still get value. Finances are shared openly to build trust with attendees.

The organizers' children then take the stage to describe growing up around the event. They list the physical chores they did, including stuffing bags, folding shirts, and building badges, and the skills they picked up, such as streaming talks and editing media. Their takeaways are to build a community, keep asking questions, stay willing to learn, and treat others with kindness, even when you disagree.

talks.title: Extracting the Ghost in the Machine
talks.teaser: Surveys how attackers poison, invert and evade machine learning models, from prompt injection to adversarial patches.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with prompt injection, where crafted input gets a chatbot to ignore its rules and expose system prompts, internal records or private notes, including through tricks such as markdown image links that leak data. The speaker argues this matters because training data and hidden instructions can contain healthcare, financial and credential information.

The middle section moves from prompts to the models themselves. Data poisoning means slipping a small number of crafted or mislabelled samples into a training set, which can steer a model's behaviour; examples from assessments included a résumé screener and a code-sharing platform that could be made to return malicious code. Model inversion works in reverse, reconstructing faces and other private details from a model by querying it, even without direct access to its weights. Adversarial patches and subtle noise overlays push vision systems toward a different label, such as a toaster or a stop sign, and can be tuned to be nearly invisible to people. The speaker also described a hiding attack that suppresses a person's label, and a check-reading system whose amount could be misread.

The closing point is that these techniques are still early in research, and that the range of possible attacks is limited mainly by imagination. For practitioners, the takeaway is to treat training data, model outputs and any exposed query interface as part of the attack surface when assessing AI systems.

talks.title: Casting Light on Shadow Cloud Deployments
talks.teaser: Shows how a triage tool maps exposed AWS resources to answer early incident response questions quickly.
talks.summary:
Incident responders often find cloud systems that were launched informally: proofs of concept that became production, test copies sitting in dev accounts, or staff who opened an account outside any governance process. Once a service has a public IP address, it becomes an initial access point. The talk walks through a 2024 campaign against an exposed Jenkins server at a bank, where attackers exploited a file inclusion flaw, read stored credentials, and reached customer data through a supply chain path. It also covers a small company whose publicly reachable database was wiped and held for ransom.

The speakers argue that existing cloud posture tools focus on long-term configuration, while responders need fast answers about which resources are affected, who owns them, how long they were exposed, which services are involved, and whether the problem is isolated. They present Luminant, an open tool that starts from AWS network interfaces with public addresses and works outward to security groups, instances and load balancers. It pulls CloudTrail and AWS Config history for context and checks what the internet can see using Nmap and Shodan. A live demo showed permissive rules, a change timeline and a fingerprinted Grafana version.

The main takeaways are to validate scanner findings, since IP addresses get recycled, and to use allow lists and tag-based exclusions to cut noise. Output is available in terminal, HTML, JSON and CSV timeline formats. The tool runs in Docker and needs read-only AWS permissions, and the speakers urge attendees to review the code before running it in their own environments.

talks.title: Pages from a Sword Makers Notebook pt 3 The cursed blade
talks.teaser: Shows how a Go Mimikatz packer with a hidden build-time backdoor exposed the machines of those who used it.
talks.summary:
The speaker, presenting remotely, recounts a Go-based wrapper they wrote years earlier for Mimikatz, the credential-dumping tool. The wrapper worked in stages: a packer fetched a Mimikatz release, split the binary into two random pads that XOR back together, and used a shellcode loader to run it from memory. A small "fixer" step marked every binary section as executable, which Go's runtime would normally reject, and that choice largely slipped past antivirus scanning.

When the speaker noticed a third party repeatedly uploading the tool to VirusTotal, they shipped an update containing a backdoor. At build time it collected host details such as usernames, environment variables, monitor screenshots and the public IP address, encrypted the data with a static key and embedded it in the binary, so nothing was sent over the network. Over roughly a year, samples returned to VirusTotal carried data from many build machines. The speaker walks through those machines and what they suggest about the operators, linking usernames and IP ranges to organizations and regions, though many of these links are offered as inference rather than confirmed fact.

The story ends when the operators found comments in the source code and worked out what had happened. The speaker then removed the backdoor and changed the cryptography to evade detection again. The practical lessons are that data can be hidden inside shipped binaries, that Go binaries can sidestep signature-based scanning, and that public sandbox uploads can reveal the environments of the people who build and run tools.

talks.title: ESkyScan Autonomously Filming Aircraft
talks.teaser: Shows how to build a low-cost ADS-B system that automatically points a PTZ camera at passing aircraft.
talks.summary:
This talk presents Skyscan, a project from a rapid prototyping group that automatically films aircraft broadcasting their position. The speakers begin with ADS-B, the transponder system used across civil aviation, which sends position, speed and heading in the clear. It can be received with an inexpensive software defined radio and decoder software. Aircraft ownership can be looked up in FAA registry records, with crowdsourced databases as a fallback, though trustees and LLCs often obscure the real owner.

The hardware is modest: a pan-tilt-zoom security camera, a small single-board computer or laptop, and power-over-Ethernet wiring, for roughly $500 with the camera making up most of the cost. The software converts each aircraft's coordinates into azimuth and elevation relative to the camera, then interpolates between sparse and delayed updates so the motion looks smooth. Targets are prioritized by distance or interest, and the system is containerized and published on GitHub. Careful leveling of the camera matters, since small orientation errors affect tracking.

The speakers argued that a long archive of imagery builds a baseline of normal air traffic, which helps analysts spot anomalies such as unexplained drone reports. Labels from FAA records could also be used to train image classifiers for aircraft types. They closed by inviting attendees to build the system and to talk with them afterward.

talks.title: Inside the Information Stealer Ecosystem
talks.teaser: Traces how infostealer malware harvests credentials and session cookies, and how the Redline operation was disrupted.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with what information stealers are: remote access trojans that copy saved browser credentials, session cookies, autofill data, and files from a victim's machine, then send them to criminal servers. Stolen session cookies can let attackers bypass multi-factor authentication. The speakers walk through the stealer economy, including Telegram channels that give away or sell logs, malware-as-a-service pricing, and a fake AI tool download that led one victim to ransomware. They also show how thread actors use "checker" tools to sort logs for valuable accounts such as banking and streaming.

The middle section covers the Redline and Meta takedown. The operators first made a mistake by signing their control panel and malware with the same certificate, which allowed a revocation. They then moved licensing to a GitHub-hosted dead drop resolver and later to Pastebin, and each single point of failure was removed in turn. Law enforcement finished the operation in October 2024. The team also tested what a stealer can take in practice: file grabbers collect small documents, a browser authenticator extension's secrets could regenerate valid one-time codes, while Bitwarden and Dashlane stored little usable data locally. KeePass vaults mainly mattered when the master password was weak.

The closing section looks at Chrome's application-bound encryption and the bypasses that followed. The speakers argue it raises the cost of theft and leaves noisier traces that detection and incident response can use. Their practical advice: avoid cracked software, never disable antivirus, keep work machines away from family use, use a password manager and SmartScreen, and check stealer log databases for corporate accounts so exposed credentials can be reset before attackers use them.

talks.title: Azure Survey 60 million Users & Counting
talks.teaser: Shows how public Microsoft 365 endpoints expose usernames and employee availability at scale, with survey data to back it up.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a hacker at TrustedSec, presents research on user enumeration in Microsoft Azure and Microsoft 365. User enumeration lets an attacker confirm which usernames are valid, which makes password spraying and phishing easier. Microsoft does not treat this as a vulnerability and describes the information as public. The talk has two parts: a long-running OneDrive-based survey that has identified about 63 million users, and roughly six months of monitoring Teams presence data for Microsoft staff.

The survey relies only on web scraping, with no login attempts, and draws on public data sources and Microsoft discovery endpoints. Reported findings include about 1.25 million live tenant and domain combinations, ADFS use by around 42 percent of Fortune 500 companies, and common username formats such as first initial plus surname. Numeric suffixes make up about 12 percent of usernames. The Teams work uses presence enumeration, which has been enabled by default since 2014. The speaker showed how availability data can reveal calendar busy times, and collected around 52,000 out-of-office replies. A self-hosted successor tool was announced.

The speaker argues that a homogeneous cloud platform gives adversaries one concentrated attack surface, and that bug bounties are unlikely to surface serious flaws of that kind. The recommendations are for Microsoft to disable user enumeration, stop charging for security features that should be standard, and make secure defaults the norm. For defenders, the practical takeaway is to check how much tenant discovery and presence exposure their own organisation already leaves visible.

talks.title: Covert Channels Using QUIC Protocol Headers
talks.teaser: Shows how a covert channel can hide encrypted messages inside QUIC connection ID fields to evade entropy-based detection.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with background on covert channels, framing them through the prisoners problem and the Department of Defense's split between storage and timing channels. It then covers later risk measures that weigh bandwidth over time and the sensitivity of the data leaking. QUIC, the UDP-based transport beneath HTTP/3, is introduced next, and the speaker explains why its connection ID field is attractive: it is a required header with a wide allowed entropy range, so random-looking bytes there can blend in.

The middle of the talk walks through a proof of concept built as a university assignment on a Python QUIC library. Public key material and encrypted data are split into connection IDs, and short command messages such as a remote identity check are sent back and forth. The speaker compared the entropy of the carried bytes with ordinary traffic captured from real sessions, and estimated throughput at roughly 10 bytes per second, just under the old 100 bits per second threshold for high risk.

The speaker is candid about weaknesses: a parity bias from the odd-valued modulus, no authenticated key exchange, exposure to bit-flipping and man-in-the-middle attacks, and fragility when synchronization is lost. The takeaway for defenders is that a high-entropy field filled with high-entropy data is hard to spot statistically, so endpoint protection and data loss prevention controls matter. The closing advice is to build and document ideas even when they have been explored before.

talks.title: Hacker Rock & Roll
talks.teaser: Traces twenty years of ShmooCon talks and turns them into a labeled taxonomy, dataset and visualizations.
talks.summary:
The talk looks back at roughly twenty years of ShmooCon, covering about 800 talks. The speakers found the records scattered across several sources rather than in one place, so they gathered, cleaned and merged them into a single spreadsheet. The project was inspired by an art piece that charted music genres over time, which led to a similar view of the conference's themes. Fire talks were left out because the early years did not record them consistently.

To organize the material, the team built a taxonomy from the bottom up, letting the talks shape the categories, and ended with 45 top-level groups. Each talk was labeled from its title and abstract, then from the video or news coverage when those were not enough, using a majority-of-content rule for talks that span several areas. Exploitation was the largest category, with law and policy, defense, detection and intelligence also prominent. Trends shifted over time: deception topics first appeared around 2010, and new subtopics tended to follow new technologies. The graphs were drawn with Graphviz, using a Python parser that converts a tab-separated file into valid graph code.

The speakers released the dataset, the parsing code and high-resolution visualizations for download. They also noted that the corpus reflects accepted talks rather than all submissions, so it carries selection bias. Their takeaways were that volunteer archivists and archive sites deserve support, and that studying a conference's full history is a useful way to learn the field.

talks.title: The Cost of an Incident
talks.teaser: Breaks down what cyber incidents really cost organizations, from response and notification to downtime and reputation.
talks.summary:
The speaker works as a cyber risk engineer, supporting insurance underwriters who are not cyber specialists. Drawing on claims work, the talk argues that security staff struggle to win budget from leadership, and suggests a more persuasive approach: study what similar organizations lost in their own bad days and present those figures in dollars rather than security jargon.

The talk sorts incident costs into several groups. Direct costs cover containment, rebuilds, incident response firms, ransom payments, negotiator and cryptocurrency fees, and equipment that is cheaper to replace than recover. Compliance costs grow quickly when sensitive data is involved, since locating affected people in messy, poorly labeled data takes time, and notification alone can cost about a dollar per person before credit monitoring is added. Business interruption is often the largest concern, with short ransomware recoveries lasting weeks and some taking more than a year, and supplier outages can halt operations too. Regulatory investigations, legal settlements, fines, reputational damage and required upgrades, known as betterment, come later and are often not covered by insurance.

The practical takeaways focus on reducing those costs before an incident happens. Segmenting networks makes response easier, and well-meaning staff should not wipe suspect machines without responder guidance. Backups should be resistant to ransomware, stored separately, and actually restored in practice. Organizations should arrange retainers with responders and negotiators, keep a paper copy of the response plan and contacts, rehearse critical processes without the network, and prepare crisis communications. The speaker's central advice is to keep only the data needed for compliance and the business, and to plan and practice every step.

talks.title: Imposter Detection with Watchman
talks.teaser: Shows how to catch lookalike domains from public registry data before attackers start phishing or sending fake invoices.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the problem of impostor domains: lookalike names registered to phish staff or run business email compromise. Fake invoices can pass email authentication because the sending domain is technically legitimate, so they often go unnoticed in accounts payable. The speaker argues that commercial monitoring services tend to alert days or weeks after registration, even though the signal exists much earlier, and that the brand to watch is often a vendor or client rather than the organisation itself.

The middle section explains how monitoring works. Registries publish zone files listing registered domains, and the speaker describes applying for registry access through ICANN. Each day's files are compared against the previous day's, so only new registrations need processing, which avoids the slow row-by-row database inserts that a naive approach would require. Matches are found with substring or string edit distance checks. The free tool, called Watchman, is a Django application that runs on modest hardware. It also watches for MX records and live websites, enriches hits with VirusTotal data, and sends alerts to Slack.

The closing part covers limits and plans. Some registries are harder to reach, passive DNS feeds are costly, and hosting the database is the main barrier to sharing results with others. Planned work includes interactive Slack actions, safer screenshots, and seeding lists from known-good addresses. The practical takeaway is that newly registered lookalike domains can be spotted early using public data, and that defenders should watch for them before mail or web content appears.

talks.title: The Permission Slip Attack
talks.teaser: Shows how exported Android components with loose intent filters let unprivileged apps place phone calls without the call permission.
talks.summary:
The talk covers a confused deputy problem in Android, where an app holding a sensitive permission exposes a component that a separate, unprivileged app can trigger. The speaker first reviews the permission model, separating normal, runtime and signature permissions, and then compares two intents. The call action can start a phone call without user interaction and maps directly to the call phone permission, while the dial action only pre-fills the dialer. Developers who received reports often replied that the documentation required the permission, which the speaker found to be a misreading of how the platform behaves in practice.

The speaker names the pattern the permission slip attack and presents a command-line toolkit called pslip. It parses manifests for exported components, intent filters that accept call actions or script schemes, and hardcoded AES or DES keys in code. A manifest-only scan takes about five seconds, while adding JADX-based key searches can push runtime to a minute. The speaker showed real findings from recent CVE and bug bounty reports, then ran a short demo in which injected JavaScript exposed a saved password hidden behind asterisks in a browser component.

The closing advice is to stop exporting components that do not need to be exported, prefer inline permissions and tightly scoped intent filters, and avoid hardcoding keys. Custom permissions set to a normal protection level can also be granted without user consent. Questions covered how to score the issue, since opinions differ on whether a pre-installed trigger app counts as a local or network attack, and the speaker noted that a bug bounty program for Google Play had ended.

talks.title: Our Time in a Product Review Cabal
talks.teaser: Shows how a free-product review scheme exposed insecure cloud-connected smart devices, and how to inspect and harden them.
talks.summary:
The speakers explain how a postcard offering a free product, reimbursed after a purchase and review, grew into a large circle of friends receiving free smart-home gear from many sellers. Once the hardware was in hand, they set out to determine whether these cloud-connected devices were safe to run on a home network. Many products were white-label units built on a shared cloud platform, and several exposed far more than expected through serial debug ports, forced firmware updates, or video copies sent to third-party cloud hosts.

They described their assessment approach, starting with UART serial access, which often needs only a cheap adapter and pogo pins, and then packet capture to see where each device connected. Findings included an old RTSP media server with a well-known remote code execution flaw, a peer-to-peer relay design that let other users reach a camera using a guessable identifier, and a camera whose destinations shifted after an automatic update. For defense, they recommended DHCP reservations without a gateway, layer three access controls, flashing open-source firmware over serial or JTAG, or swapping a microcontroller. Devices that cannot be controlled should be discarded.

They also covered spotting fake reviews, such as uniform five-star praise, generic wording, and reviews describing a different product. A vendor that paid for product research offered a contrasting example. The main takeaways were to test devices before trusting them, check where they connect, and approach cheap cloud-tied gear with skepticism.

talks.title: Building on the Foundation of our Shared Hacker History
talks.teaser: Traces hacker culture from 19th-century lock picking and wireless hacks to MIT pranks, early hacker ethics, and today's hacker spaces.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames the talk around this year's commencement theme, arguing that looking back at the community's origins helps it move forward. He profiles historical figures who embodied the hacker mindset. Michael Faraday's years of failed experiments are set against the daily reality of penetration testing, and Alfred Hobbs's public lock-picking at the 1851 Great Exhibition shows how demonstrating weaknesses can reshape an industry.

The middle section traces the lineage through a 1903 wireless demonstration disrupted by a prankster, the Bourbaki mathematics collective that insisted on meeting in person, and the MIT hacking tradition with its unwritten conduct code. It credits the Building 26 hackers and experiments with Conway's Game of Life with shaping the early hacker ethic, then follows the path from the Hacker Manifesto and BBS culture to modern hacker spaces and the large cons. The speaker stresses that the community has no formal structure and that its in-person gatherings matter most.

The closing argument is that hacking is a mindset of curiosity, critical thinking and persistence rather than a fashion or a narrow set of skills. Knowing when failure produces progress, taking responsibility for mistakes, and sharing what you learn are presented as core habits. Newcomers are urged to attend cons, join a hacker space, and aspire to have something to say rather than simply wanting to be a speaker.

talks.title: I Just Wanted to Charge the Car
talks.teaser: Follows a home-battery owner who reverse engineers an Android app to control a solar battery's smart relay for EV charging.
talks.summary:
The speaker wanted to route surplus solar energy from a home battery into an electric car instead of selling it back to the grid. The battery vendor's gateway included a smart relay able to switch heavy loads, so the plan depended on learning how the vendor's phone app talked to that gateway. Starting from an Android build of the app, he decompiled the code, used an HTTP proxy to watch traffic, and traced the calls that drove the relay.

The investigation turned up hard-coded demo credentials, an exposed Swagger endpoint with documentation, and a shared MQTT message broker with no authorization or isolation. Login tokens were deterministic and could not be revoked, and a wildcard subscription exposed every message on the bus. He worked through disclosure with the EFF and struggled to find a security contact at the vendor. The vendor later patched by moving traffic to an HTTP endpoint with topic checks, which broke his setup until he updated it.

The takeaway is that a basic review would have caught these flaws, and that the gateway likely still runs an unisolated broker, so a deeper fix would need more than an API change. He shares working code and a Rust wrapper for the API, and suggests that vendors and researchers both need better disclosure channels.

talks.title: Hacker Non Court Seymore, Inc v ThinkIz, Inc
talks.teaser: A mock arbitration stages a dispute over liability after an eyewear joint venture's software is breached.
talks.summary:
The talk stages a mock arbitration over a fictional joint venture between a century-old eyewear maker and a small AI software startup. Smart glasses and contact lenses built by the startup were disrupted by a flaw in an open-source library, leaving wearers injured and some dead. Opening statements frame the dispute as a question of who carries responsibility for software security, and each side's counsel argues its position.

Witness examinations bring the operational failures into focus. The eyewear company's chief executive admits it had no security officer and relied on a questionnaire to review its vendor. The startup's chief executive describes handing off installation steps without verifying the open-source code, using background checks sourced from LinkedIn that missed a North Korean contractor, and hiring a forensic firm found online. Cross-examination probes whether anyone actually reviewed the code and whether the agreement assigned security duties.

The arbitrator's written decision assigns 70 percent liability to the eyewear company and 30 percent to the startup. The reasoning rests on the larger firm's failure to review the agreement, oversee its partner, and meet its medical-device obligations. The closing discussion covers FDA cybersecurity authority, HIPAA changes and how hardware fail-safe design may matter in court. Practical takeaways include weighing context, potential harm and knowledge, documenting security concerns honestly, avoiding overpromising, and not relying on insurers to cover losses.

talks.title: Shmooganography
talks.teaser: Looks behind the scenes at building a multi-stage steganography puzzle contest, including its failed stages and lessons learned.
talks.summary:
The speakers run the steganography contest that has been a fixture at ShmooCon for many years. Teams work through a multi-stage puzzle in which each stage yields a code word and a clue. The game is coordinated by email rather than a booth, and the speakers explain how it began as a small solo project with hidden codes slipped into printed pens and grew into a five-stage game with prizes and sponsors.

The middle of the talk covers how the game is built: logistics, technique design, and deployment, all tied to a yearly theme such as Magic: The Gathering cards, The Legend of Zelda, or Stargate. Examples include UV-printed posters, a display that needs polarized glasses to read, a USB-based stage, data hidden in JPEG streams, and a Wi-Fi capture that could not be broadcast live. They also describe failures, including an infrared stage with LEDs too weak to show the message, a light-based stage that needed a black tablecloth, and overlapping media that confused teams. Backup plans, such as distributing the capture file, kept those stages playable.

The speakers close by reflecting on the effort involved, the value players get from the challenge, and the uncertainty about what follows, since this is the final year under the current name. For practitioners running puzzle or CTF-style games, the takeaways are to avoid single shared bottlenecks, keep stages visibly distinct, and plan for deployment failures before they happen.

talks.title: The Hardest Problem I’ve Ever Seen
talks.teaser: Explains why securing US election outcomes is so hard, and how risk-limiting audits help verify results despite flawed software.
talks.summary:
Matt Blaze opens by describing how US elections are run: mostly by counties and townships, under state law, with budgets competing against everyday local services. He stresses two uncomfortable facts. Real technical vulnerabilities exist in parts of election infrastructure, yet no credible evidence has ever shown a technical attack changing a US election outcome.

He traces the path from the 2000 Florida recount, where punch-card ballots and hanging chads became a national embarrassment, to the Help America Vote Act. That law pushed jurisdictions toward paper-based optical scan systems and touchscreen machines. Software-driven direct recording machines brought new trust problems, because voters cannot read their own votes and software failures can quietly alter results.

The central argument is that software is unreliable, so election systems should be designed so that a software flaw cannot cause an unrecoverable wrong outcome. Ron Rivest's idea of software independence, and Philip Stark's risk-limiting audits, show how hand-checking a small random sample of paper ballots can bound the risk of a wrong result. Blaze closes by urging technologists to help local officials, consider becoming election workers, and help retire paperless touchscreen machines.

talks.title: TaskMooster 2
talks.teaser: Follows four contestants through timed, offbeat challenges set by a task master in a live comedy game show.
talks.summary:
This is the second part of a comedy game show recorded as a ShmooCon 2025 side event, in which four contestants compete through a series of timed, offbeat tasks set by a task master. The episode opens with a standings recap and an unplanned incident involving a plush moose that fell down a stairwell before filming began. The first challenge is building the tallest contiguous pile of moose using tape, string and whatever else the contestants could find. Heights are measured after each build, and the task master rules that loosely arranged animals do not count as a pile.

The middle section covers a paper airplane contest, scored on distance and decoration and flown on a runway borrowed for the day. Judging calls drive much of the humour: an audience vote decides whether one contestant's creation counts as a plane, and the task master settles how distances are measured. The final live task is Spellukon, a group spelling game whose rules are replaced again and again as the show goes on. Several contestants are eliminated for breaking the rules, and one is out after a dispute over what counts as a valid phonetic alphabet.

The episode closes with final tallies: Jesse finishes first with 15 points, ahead of Heidi with 13, Rob with 12 and Allan with 9. The organizers thank the volunteers who ran the production and hand out novelty prizes. There is no technical security content here. Its value is as a lighthearted record of a conference side event, showing how a playful, low-stakes activity can be run with clear, if sometimes contested, rules.

talks.title: The UN Cybercrime Treaty is Final, Heres What You Need to Know
talks.teaser: Explains the final UN cybercrime treaty's offenses, safeguards and gaps, and what security researchers can do about them.
talks.summary:
Kurt Opsahl, an internet lawyer with long ties to the Electronic Frontier Foundation, explains the final text of the United Nations cybercrime convention. He traces its origins to a 2019 committee, its aim to replace the 2001 Budapest Convention, and the fights over human rights language that stayed in the text despite opposition.

The core of the talk walks through the offenses: illegal access, interception, data and system interference, misuse of devices, forgery and fraud. Opsahl stresses that protections useful to researchers, such as dishonest-intent requirements and harm thresholds, are optional for member states. He flags risks for pentesters carrying dual-use tools, password sharing, agents acting for users, VPN-style spoofing, and duties that could force people with system knowledge to help access encrypted data.

He closes with the ratification path: signatures in Hanoi, forty states to take effect, and a two-thirds Senate vote in the US, where a non-binding statement opposing bad-faith requests may not outlast a change in administration. His advice is to press for safeguards or oppose signing, watch the deferred content-crimes protocol, and contact legislators directly. Audience questions covered tool possession, intent and dark patterns.

talks.title: Impos73r Future Breaches & Past Disasters
talks.teaser: Describes how volunteer IT teams restore connectivity to communities after disasters and how to join the ITDRC.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces the Information Technology Disaster Resource Center, a volunteer nonprofit founded around 2008 that sends people and equipment to communities whose connectivity has been cut off by disasters. The speaker, a regional deputy director who also works as a security engineer, outlines the group's history, its partnerships with technology companies, and its reach across FEMA regions.

The middle section covers field work. Examples include a training exercise in New York that simulated a grid-down scenario, using a cellular backhaul, mesh access points and a wireless bridge to cross a gorge. Other deployments included a Wi-Fi project for underserved rural areas, support for the Baltimore bridge collapse response, and hurricane work in Florida, where sites ranged from donation warehouses to a repurposed prison. A recurring lesson was that plans rarely survive contact with a site, so troubleshooting and improvising are the most valuable skills. The remote response team provides situational awareness, logistics and help desk support, while a newer cyber incident support team helps government, education and utility organizations recover after attacks.

To close, the speaker explained how to get involved: apply through the volunteer page, complete background checks and onboarding, and take FEMA incident management courses. In Q&A, the speaker said volunteers generally do not receive employer pay protections unless their company partners with the group, and that deployment templates are adjusted for each site. The takeaway is that skilled defenders can donate their time to help communities and organizations get back online.

talks.title: Firetalks
talks.teaser: Short talks cover careers, SOC humor, the hobo code, statistics, malware storage and bypassing a ticket captcha.
talks.summary:
Firetalks is the short-talk contest held during ShmooCon 2025. Each speaker gets roughly fifteen minutes, a panel of judges scores the talks with playful rubrics, and the audience contributes donations and light-hearted bribes. The host traces the event back to 2009, notes that this is its last run at ShmooCon, and thanks past judges, volunteers and speakers who kept it going.

The lineup ranges widely. One speaker links the old hobo code to the security community's habit of helping peers find work and resist burnout. Another offers a career framework that treats a job search like reconnaissance against a target. A SOC analyst describes using memes, fake passwords and decoy files to stress-test alerts and wake up tired teams. A statistics talk argues that distributions communicate uncertainty better than single averages in security reports. A malware researcher introduces an open-source database that stores samples and finds similar files with fuzzy hashes. The final talk shows how a small local language model can solve the ticket site's text captcha, and how a route announcement could redirect traffic to the registration server, along with defenses such as per-user URLs.

For practitioners, the session is a reminder that short, focused talks can carry useful ideas. The detection testing, the uncertainty-aware reporting and the community-building advice are easy to adapt, while the ticketing demo doubles as a case study in weak rate limiting and cleartext traffic.

talks.title: Tracking the Triad Nexus
talks.teaser: Traces the Funnel CDN's CNAME chains and leased IP space used to host scam and gambling sites.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the 2024 Polyfill.io supply chain attack, in which a widely embedded JavaScript domain redirected some mobile visitors to low-quality casino sites. The domain's new owner was Funnel, a China-linked content delivery network tied to gambling businesses. Revisiting a 2022 pig-butchering investigation, the research team found sites from that campaign still live two years later, suggesting takedown complaints had failed.

The middle of the talk explains how the network hides itself. Funnel chains CNAME records, changes its alias domains over time, and resolves them to pools of IP addresses spread across many autonomous systems, including blocks leased from major Western hosts. A shared error page helped map the footprint. Clustering casino sites by scripts, page titles, favicons and a referenced code repository suggested one developer built many fake brand sites. Linked Telegram channels and money-movement language pointed to a wider laundering scheme, and one CNAME served only retail phishing and investment scams.

The speaker closes with open questions about the financial impact, why gambling sites stayed online while misusing brand names, and who ultimately controls the network. For practitioners, the takeaway is that blocking an entire cloud range can cause collateral damage, so tracking the naming and DNS layers matters as much as individual IPs.

talks.title: TaskMooster 1
talks.teaser: Contestants compete in silly gift and carnival-game challenges while a host keeps score for the crowd.
talks.summary:
This ShmooCon 2025 segment is a comedy game show rather than a technical presentation. Host Bryson Bort keeps score, and the audience is asked to help keep the contestants on schedule.

The first round asks each contestant to bring a last-minute gift that answers a prompt. The gifts range from a branded flask holster and a plane-spotting guide to a novelty item with a long regifting history. The contestants score one another, and Jesse takes the early lead.

The second round is a set of carnival-style games: ring toss, darts, and a task of knocking down cans with tennis balls, scored toward 100 points. Rule-bending moves become part of the debate about who should win. After both rounds, Rob has seven points and holds first place. The segment ends with a promise to finish the contest on Sunday. For a practitioner, the main takeaway is that this is a community moment rather than a lesson.

talks.title: I'm Not Your Enemy How Practitioners Can Empower Content
talks.teaser: Shows how security practitioners and marketers can team up to turn research into credible, buyer-relevant content.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a content marketer at a security company, opens with a friction most technical teams will recognise. Practitioners are busy and often see marketing content as fluff, while marketers lack the findings and customer insight needed to write something useful. She argues that the answer is closer collaboration, with practitioners sharing what prospects struggle with and marketers doing the research work that engineers rarely have time for.

To make the case, she walks through a campaign that started with a question on a fan forum about whether an online shop was legitimate. Using domain intelligence tooling, she reviewed reputation scores, the registration country and frequent certificate changes. Colleagues then recognised the domain from a separate investigation that uncovered a wider fraud operation, with rotating domains impersonating well-known retail brands. Her research was less technical than theirs, but it suited finance and legal readers who influence purchasing decisions and need the business impact rather than the details.

Her takeaway is that generic, keyword-driven articles are losing credibility, so bespoke research grounded in real findings will matter more. Practitioner input also builds trust with sales and product teams and opens conversations with prospects. In the example she describes, a customer used the published piece to justify buying the product, which she presents as a direct link between this kind of collaboration and revenue.

talks.title: Books, OMG, Books Commence with Reading
talks.teaser: Shares how to start and run a book club, from picking titles and discussion questions to building community around reading.
talks.summary:
Meghan Jacquot opens by asking why anyone would want to launch or take part in a book club. She links the idea to the sense of community that forms at conferences and argues that discussing what you read with peers from different backgrounds keeps you learning in a fast-moving field.

The middle of the talk covers how to run one. She describes two clubs she belongs to: a bimonthly online science fiction group focused on cyberpunk novels that also meets in person once a year at DEF CON, and a non-fiction group that alternates narrative books with technical ones. She outlines formats, from choosing titles months or a year ahead to using fixed questions, questions drawn from the discussion, or prompts borrowed from reading guides. Sample questions ask whether you liked a book, whether you would recommend it, what it taught you, and who it was written for.

She then walks through three reading themes. "Keep the receipts" covers forensics and investigation stories. "Use it or lose it" covers technical books paired with exercises and examples that authors publish online, so readers can practise skills. The fiction theme focuses on characters who push back against inequity and survival pressure, which she ties to community resilience. She closes by challenging attendees to meet someone new and stay involved with other events, and points them to her book lists and QR codes.

talks.title: ShmooFAQ
talks.teaser: Quizzes the crowd in multiple-choice rounds on hacker history, networking, math and pop-culture trivia.
talks.summary:
ShmooFAQ is a live trivia contest held during ShmooCon 2025 in Washington. Teams of up to five people answer multiple-choice questions on paper answer sheets across several rounds, each with its own subject and test ID. The hosts run the event with heavy crowd interaction and a short list of rules, including no shouting out answers and no devices during rounds.

The questions range widely in difficulty. Early rounds cover basic facts about the conference, classic computing and networking, such as common ports, binary arithmetic and protocol names. Later rounds move into arts and literature, drawing on hacker-themed novels and films, then the history of the field and its landmark incidents, then science covering electronics and word plurals. A final round uses certification-style questions. Technical glitches interrupted the show partway through, and a side fundraiser for the Electronic Frontier Foundation ran alongside the contest.

When the scores were tallied, the winning team was announced and the audience was credited with raising more than $1,500 for the EFF. For a practitioner, the main value is social: a low-stakes way to test general knowledge, meet the community and spot gaps in fundamentals. The content is trivia rather than explanation, so it offers little technical depth.

talks.title: Murthy v Missouri
talks.teaser: Explains the Supreme Court's Murthy v Missouri ruling on government jawboning of platforms and what it means for online speech.
talks.summary:
A lawyer who files amicus briefs and writes about internet law opens by stating that the talk is education, not legal advice. The first part covers the free speech clause of the First Amendment: it restricts what the government can do to speech, while private parties such as event organizers and online platforms can decide what to host, moderate, or be associated with.

The middle section explains jawboning, where officials pressure a third party to suppress speech they cannot reach directly. It contrasts NRA v. Vullo, where a regulator's threats to insurers were held unconstitutional, with Moody v. NetChoice, which confirmed that platforms have their own editorial rights. It then turns to Murthy v. Missouri, where plaintiffs alleged federal agencies pushed platforms to remove posts. The Court found the plaintiffs lacked standing because they could not show that government coercion caused their injuries. The speaker argues that ordinary conversations between agencies and platforms remain legitimate and useful, especially where agencies hold security or public health expertise.

The closing looks ahead. The case may return to a lower court, related suits are ongoing, and coercion could still happen under future administrations. The speaker also raises whether a private company could become a state actor if government involvement grew close enough. The takeaway for practitioners is that the First Amendment limits government action rather than private choices, and that the line between persuasion and coercion is what determines whether a case has merit.

talks.title: Is this Fake? Content Provenance Tech to Fight Online Disinformation
talks.teaser: Explains how cryptographically signed content credentials like C2PA can help verify whether online images and videos are authentic.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with a familiar problem: AI-generated images, audio and video are now easy to make and are being used for pranks, personal revenge, and election interference. Detectors tend to lag behind new generators, so the speaker argues for the opposite approach, which is to attest cryptographically to genuine content at the point of creation.

The main example is C2PA, a coalition of technology companies, news organizations and camera makers that defines content credentials. A credential is a digital signature embedded in an asset, and it works like a change log: a camera signs a capture using a key stored in its hardware, and each editing tool that touches the file verifies the previous signatures and appends its own signed entry. Because the signatures follow the same certificate model as web PKI, forging a history requires private keys. The hard part is trust establishment, meaning deciding which devices, software and newsrooms get to sign. The speaker showed a browser extension that checks signed images on a web page, and noted that a BBC clip carried a valid signature while a social media repost showed a different signer.

The talk then turns to privacy. Signing everything leaves a traceable record, and journalists or whistleblowers may need to prove origin without being identified. The speaker presented zero-knowledge proofs, released in a library called Crescent, that let someone prove attributes such as employment or age without revealing identity, and described redacting exact times or locations in signed metadata. In the question period, critics raised concerns about industry leadership and specification weaknesses. The speaker responded that a newer specification version addressed public critiques, that the trust-list process is still incomplete, and that retractions would follow existing newsroom practice. For practitioners, the takeaway is that provenance will roll out over years, and its value depends on trust lists and key governance.
